[Document reproduit : dépliant publicitaire « Lake Eden Inn and Cottages », 1939]
LAKE EDEN INN AND COTTAGES
Owned and Operated by BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE, Black Mountain · North Carolina
Just off U. S. 70, near Mount Mitchell, Eastern America’s highest peak. Fourteen miles east of Asheville, four miles west of Black Mountain.
The 1939 season is from June 5 to September 9.
[Photographie :] Mount Mitchell, altitude 6711 feet.
ACCOMMODATIONS
Lake Eden is designed and managed to provide accommodations suited to the individual wishes of its guests. Rooms may be had in one of the main lodges near the dining room, beach, and tennis courts, or in one of six separate cottages. All the buildings are completely equipped with baths, modern conveniences, and comfortable living rooms with large open fireplaces.
RATES
Rates, including room, meals, and either private or connecting bath, range from $23 to $25 a week, and $3.50 to $4 a day for single guests; from $17.50 to $25 a week per guest for two or more in a room. Cottages are available for those desiring such accomodation for $75 a week, meals included, for a party of three, with additional charge for additional guests. A 10 per cent reduction is made for those staying more than four weeks.
[Carte :] “Land of the Sky” — The All Year Playground — The Great Smoky Mountain National Park.
Lake Eden Inn and Cottages publicity flyer, 1939.

[Document reproduit : texte dactylographié de David Weinrib, « The Farm »]
The Farm.
Instead of gym we took Farm. The farm was also thought of as a money making vehicle. Chicken, vegetables and beef (not too aged and thus a little tough, although the cooks did a great job stewing it in beer) also came to the college table. Paul Williams later on, gave money to the college to develop a beef herd for income. One long difficult winter when we eliminated the winter term we ate some of it, steaks instead of salary for the faculty. The farm manager worked very hard and devotedly. A few students who stayed on after worked full time on the farm.
Potter David Weinrib’s “The Farm,” undated.
Bernhard Laursen, teacher of farming, gymnastics, and folk dancing and farm manager at the Asheville Farm School.
